notes: Edition composed by Claude from the collected headlines, reading titles and metadata only.
Each narrative is an idea that joins several different events; what it joins is listed at the top. It commits to a claim, and the last rung of every narrative is the case against it. Read both.
Where a narrative continues one from the previous edition it says what has changed since; every edition is kept, so the reader can step back to where we were.

Each narrative ends with 'How we got here': four horizons, since 2020, since 2008, since 1989 and since 1945, each the start of a regime the headlines are living inside, and sometimes a fifth that reaches further back and names its own starting year. They are a trajectory, not a verdict.

Each narrative sets one or two things to watch for: what should follow, by when, if its join is right. Later editions check them against their headlines; the ledger is data/watch.json and the count stands beside the narrative's firmness.

Each narrative looks ahead: the precedent its join most resembles, two or three paths with one favoured, and where the trajectory points over a decade. That is the writer's anticipation, drawn on what it knows of history and not only on the headlines; the expectations are the earliest dated signs of the favoured path, and are how the site checks it.
The connections are made by the model, not by the publishers. Follow any headline to the original report before repeating it.
Books and trajectories appear only where they change how a fragment or a horizon reads.

readings.line: With Hormuz shut, the war's cost falls on energy importers and its gains go to producers whose oil does not pass the strait.
readings.kicker: A STRAIT / WHO PAYS / WHO GAINS

watch.what: A Gulf producer announces new or larger export capacity by pipeline or port that avoids the Strait of Hormuz.
watch.because: If the war's gains go to oil that avoids the strait, other Gulf producers should move to buy the position Aramco is now enlarging.

watch.what: The EU or a European government signs a new long-term oil or gas supply deal with a producer outside the Gulf, citing the Hormuz closure.
watch.because: Buyers paying the extra bill should move their contracts towards sellers whose cargoes do not need the strait.

ahead.precedent: The closest case is the tanker war of 1984 to 1988, when Iran and Iraq attacked shipping in the Gulf, Saudi Arabia leaned on its new East-West pipeline to Yanbu on the Red Sea, and North Sea and Alaskan oil sold to buyers who wanted barrels from elsewhere. Then the strait was harassed but stayed open, and prices fell after 1986 because of a glut. Now the strait is reported shut, and the United States is itself a large exporter, so the gain runs to American and Brazilian producers as well as to Saudi Arabia.

paths.name: Bypass routes expand and stay
paths.text: Over the next six months Aramco, the UAE and Oman add capacity that does not depend on Hormuz, and European buyers sign longer contracts with Atlantic suppliers. Even if the strait reopens, the new routes and contracts remain, because buyers who paid this year's premium will pay for insurance against the next closure. The headlines already show the first step in Aramco's pipeline work and Oman's new agreements.
paths.sign: A Gulf producer or the EU announces a pipeline, port or supply contract that does not depend on the strait.

paths.name: A deal reopens the strait
paths.text: Qatar's mediation produces an agreement within weeks, Iran lets ships pass and prices fall, so the transfer from importers to bypass sellers narrows. This is less likely soon because Iran's officials say the strait stays shut and the US is still striking Iranian targets.
paths.sign: Iran announces that commercial ships may pass through the Strait of Hormuz.

paths.name: Importers cap the price together
paths.text: The EU and Asian buyers agree a joint cap or joint purchase to hold down what they pay. Europe tried a price cap on Russian oil after 2022, but a cap on sellers it depends on is much harder to enforce.
paths.sign: EU energy ministers agree a cap or joint purchasing scheme for oil or gas imports.

ahead.decade: Over ten years oil and gas trade points towards routes that avoid the Gulf's chokepoint, with Atlantic producers taking a larger share of Europe's imports and Gulf producers paying for pipelines to other seas.

readings.claim: Fortune and Anadolu report that the closure of the Strait of Hormuz has added $142 billion, or €127 billion, to Europe's energy bill, while Saudi Aramco reports higher profits and starts expanding its East-West pipeline, Brazil sets a record for oil and gas output, and China and Brunei sign new agreements with Oman. American swing voters and Chilean drivers are pricing the same fuel into their votes and their budgets. The war is moving money according to geography: buyers everywhere pay the higher price, and the sellers who gain most are those whose oil reaches the sea without passing the strait. Saudi Arabia's Red Sea pipeline, Oman's coast on the Gulf of Oman and Brazil's Atlantic fields all lie outside it.

events.label: Strait stays shut as US strikes Iran
Europe's extra energy bill
Aramco profits and pipeline expansion
Record oil and gas output in Brazil
China and Brunei sign with Oman
Fuel costs for US voters and Chilean drivers

fragments.label: Europe's extra cost
fragments.text: Fortune (United States) reports that the Hormuz closure has cost Europe an extra $142 billion for the same energy it was already buying. Anadolu (Turkey) puts the rise in the EU's fuel bill at €127 billion. Both figures measure a higher price on the same volume, not more energy.

fragments.label: The strait stays closed
fragments.text: Walla (Israel) quotes a senior Iranian saying Iran will not open the Strait of Hormuz. WSLS (United States) reports American strikes on Iranian targets in the strait, and the NZ Herald reports Trump confirming them while Iran's president Pezeshkian urges against a return to war.

fragments.label: Voters and drivers
fragments.text: NPR reports swing voters adding high petrol prices into their choice on midterm day, and Pennsylvania voters saying Trump has not delivered lower prices. La Tercera (Chile) lists the discounts that can save drivers money on fuel in November.

fragments.label: Aramco
fragments.text: WSLS reports that higher oil prices have lifted Saudi Aramco's profits despite disruption from attacks. Al Jazeera's Arabic site reports that Aramco has begun expansion work on its East-West pipeline, which carries crude across Saudi Arabia to the Red Sea.

fragments.label: Brazil and Oman
fragments.text: Observador (Portugal) reports that oil and natural gas production in Brazil has reached a new record. Xinhua and Al Jazeera report a $4.5 billion currency swap between China and Oman, and Arab News reports Oman and Brunei raising their ties to a strategic partnership.

fragments.label: Routes rather than reserves
fragments.text: The sellers in these headlines have one thing in common: their oil leaves without passing Hormuz. The East-West pipeline ends at Yanbu on the Red Sea, Oman's export terminals face the Gulf of Oman, and Brazil's fields are in the Atlantic. Producers whose only exits are inside the Gulf do not appear among the winners. The war is paying a premium to whoever controls a route around the strait, and Aramco's pipeline work is an investment in that premium.

fragments.label: The largest buyer settles terms
fragments.text: China is the main buyer of Oman's crude, and a currency swap lets the two settle trade in yuan and rials. Signed while the strait is shut, it ties the largest importer to a supplier outside the closure. Europe, which pays in dollars and euros and has no such supplier on its doorstep, carries the bill Fortune and Anadolu describe.

fragments.label: Price, not route
fragments.text: Aramco's profit comes from the higher price, and Saudi Arabia still ships much of its oil from terminals inside the Gulf; WSLS says it earned more despite attacks, not because of its pipeline. Brazil's record is the result of a decade of offshore investment and would have come this year without a war. The Oman-Brunei partnership is not about oil at all, and China has signed dozens of currency swaps in quiet years. What the events do not share: Europe's bill is a price effect, Brazil's record is planned volume, and Oman's agreements are diplomacy whose terms the headlines do not give.

fragments.label: The US is on both sides
fragments.text: The American voters in NPR's reports pay more, but the United States is the world's largest oil producer and its companies gain from the same price. Al Jazeera frames the midterms around the cost of living in general, not fuel alone, so the voter stories may say more about inflation than about the strait.

horizons.label: Since 2020
horizons.text: When Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022, the European Union set out to end its imports of Russian pipeline gas and crude. It replaced them with liquefied gas by ship, much of it from the United States and a share from Qatar, whose cargoes leave through the Strait of Hormuz. The EU's embargo on Russian seaborne crude from December 2022 and the G7 price cap moved Europe's oil buying towards Norway, the United States, West Africa and the Gulf. In the early 2020s Europe swapped a supplier it feared for a route it could not control. The twelve-day war of June 2025, ended by American bombers at Fordow, showed that route at risk; by these headlines it is now shut, and the extra $142 billion that Fortune reports is partly the price of that earlier substitution. Over the same years Brazil and Guyana became the fastest-growing producers outside OPEC, which is why a Brazilian output record belongs to the same account.

horizons.label: Since 2008
horizons.text: The financial crisis of 2008 coincided with the start of horizontal drilling and fracking at scale in Texas and North Dakota. Within a decade American crude output had more than doubled. Congress lifted the forty-year ban on crude exports in December 2015, and by 2020 the United States was a net exporter of petroleum for the first time since the 1940s. In 2006 and 2007 Petrobras found the pre-salt fields off Rio de Janeiro, and their output, which grew after 2010, is what Observador's record reports. The Atlantic became an exporters' ocean. In September 2019 drones and missiles halved Saudi output at Abqaiq for days, and buyers began to value barrels from far away. This is why the American voters paying more at the pump in NPR's reports live in a country that also earns more from the same war: the shale years made the United States both a buyer and a seller.

horizons.label: Since 1989
horizons.text: After Iraq invaded Kuwait in August 1990, the United States made itself guarantor of the Gulf's sea lanes, basing the Fifth Fleet in Bahrain from 1995. Free passage through Hormuz became an American service that Europe and Asia used without paying for it. Meanwhile China, a net oil exporter until 1993, became the world's largest crude importer by 2017, and Oman, whose terminals lie outside the strait, came to send most of its crude to Chinese refineries. Oman also made itself the region's quiet channel, hosting the secret US-Iran contacts of 2013 that led to the nuclear agreement of 2015. The currency swap Xinhua reports and the Brunei partnership in Arab News rest on that position: a seller outside the closure, trusted by both sides, with China as its main customer. The invasion of Iraq in 2003 and the American exit from the nuclear deal in 2018 are the steps that led from the American guarantee to the strikes WSLS reports now.

horizons.label: Since 1945
horizons.text: In February 1945 Roosevelt met Ibn Saud on a cruiser in the Great Bitter Lake and traded American protection for access to Saudi oil. The company that grew from that bargain, Aramco, was wholly Saudi-owned by 1980. The embargo of 1973 showed importers that a regional war becomes a world price, and the revolution in Tehran in 1979, followed by the Iran-Iraq war, showed that the strait itself could be threatened. Saudi Arabia's answer was the East-West pipeline, completed in 1981 to carry crude across the peninsula to Yanbu on the Red Sea, so that its exports would not depend on Hormuz. The expansion Al Jazeera reports is that decision being enlarged forty-five years later. Daniel Yergin's The Prize describes a century in which the location of a barrel mattered as much as its price, and this week's headlines read the same way, with the gain going to oil that can leave by another sea.

readings.line: Large breaches now start with a firm's suppliers or its staff rather than its own systems, and the firm still bears the loss.

watch.what: An investigator, retailer or supplier says the European supermarket attacks entered through a refrigeration or maintenance contractor's remote access.
watch.because: The join holds that the way in is a party the victim trusts, so the supermarket attacks should trace to a supplier as the airline and city breaches did.

watch.what: A second company or crypto exchange reports a theft or breach that began with a fake recruiter, job offer or job interview.
watch.because: If hiring has become a route in, the Binance method will be found in other firms rather than remain a single case.

ahead.precedent: The closest case is the Target breach of late 2013, when attackers used the network login of a Pennsylvania heating and refrigeration contractor to reach the retailer's tills and took 40 million card numbers. American retailers then separated vendor access from payment systems and moved to chip cards within two years. The present differs in scale and in effect: the supermarket attacks change what machines do, so food is thrown away, rather than data being copied.

paths.name: Rules move to the suppliers
paths.text: Over the next three to six months European cyber agencies and retail groups require refrigeration and maintenance firms to log or cut remote access to store equipment, and exchanges tighten rules on staff running software from recruiters. Because every case here runs through a third party, the cheapest fix is at the supplier, and Italy's advice to check supplier contacts is the first version of it.
paths.sign: A national cyber agency or retail association issues rules on remote access by maintenance or refrigeration suppliers.

paths.name: A state is named
paths.text: The EU or a member government attributes the supermarket attacks to a Russian-linked or North Korean group, and the question becomes one of sanctions rather than supplier rules. Pyongyang's denial over Binance shows attribution is already being argued, but European governments have been slow to name authors of attacks on shops.
paths.sign: The EU or a European government names a state or group as responsible for the supermarket attacks.

paths.name: Firms take systems back in-house
paths.text: Large retailers or airlines end contracts with outside vendors and bring control of equipment and data back under their own staff. The cost and the shortage of skilled staff make this rare.
paths.sign: A large retailer or airline announces it is ending an outside vendor's access after a breach.

ahead.decade: Over ten years the duty to secure systems points down the supply chain, so that maintenance firms, recruiters and software vendors carry audit obligations that until now fell on banks and airlines.

readings.change: The previous edition joined what was being hit: shop freezers and an exchange's wallets. Today's headlines say how the attackers got in: the Binance theft is reported to have begun with a fake job interview of an engineer, Singapore Airlines' records were reached through Amadeus, and Italian advice tells shops to check contacts with suppliers. The supermarket attacks have spread to Belgium, where a store discarded food, and to Greece.
readings.claim: O Globo, El Mundo and Yle report that the $6.3 billion theft from Binance began with a fake job interview of one of its engineers; the attacks on supermarket refrigeration have spread to Belgium and Greece, and Italian advice tells shops to check their contacts with suppliers; Singapore Airlines says 46,000 booking records were reached through the travel technology firm Amadeus; and Osaka City names may have leaked from a distribution service it used. In each case the attacker did not break the victim's own systems but came in through a person or contractor the victim relied on. The defences that firms built around their own networks are not where these breaches start, and the losses still fall on the firm whose name is in the headline.

events.label: Binance theft began with fake job interview
Supermarket refrigeration attacks spread in Europe
SIA records exposed through Amadeus
Osaka City names leaked via outside service
Russian cloud host Beget loses data
Warnings about attacks and home devices

fragments.label: A job interview
fragments.text: O Globo (Brazil) reports that the $6.3 billion theft from Binance began with a fake job interview scam. El Mundo (Spain) says it was set up through a job interview with one of the exchange's engineers, and Yle (Finland) says the hackers exploited a fake interview.

fragments.label: Denial and recovery
fragments.text: El Litoral (Argentina) reports that Pyongyang has denied involvement in the attack. The Star (Malaysia) reports that Binance is reopening withdrawals for more assets on several networks.

rungs.label: Shops, an airline and a city

fragments.label: Supermarket freezers
fragments.text: Liputan6 (Indonesia) reports that the hacking of European supermarkets is spreading and that a Belgian store discarded its food stock. The Star reports the refrigeration attack hitting supermarkets across Europe, and THE BEST (Greece) says it has reached Greece. Corriere della Sera (Italy) carries the advice given to shops: verify administrative accounts and check contacts with suppliers.

fragments.label: Bookings, names and cloud data
fragments.text: CNA (Singapore) reports that about 46,000 Singapore Airlines booking records were accessed in a breach at the travel technology company Amadeus. Asahi (Japan) reports that names may have leaked from a distribution service used by Osaka City after unauthorised access. Izvestia (Russia) reports that the hosting firm Beget has lost data in its cloud infrastructure.

rungs.label: The way in is a third party

fragments.label: Trusted access
fragments.text: Each victim had given access to someone outside its own control: an engineer approached as a job candidate, a booking system shared by many airlines, a mailing service used by a city, and, by the Italian advice, the suppliers who maintain store equipment. The attackers chose the point where the victim trusts by default. Singapore Airlines and Osaka City report the breach, but neither built the system that failed.

fragments.label: What the warnings point at
fragments.text: Sina (China) reports Britain's AI minister warning that a serious cyber attack in the UK is highly likely soon, and iefimerida (Greece) lists home devices from televisions to fridges that can become targets. Both describe the threat as machines. The day's actual breaches came through people and vendors, which is where the warnings say least.

fragments.label: Different crimes
fragments.text: Binance is a theft of money, the supermarket attacks are sabotage that destroys food, the Singapore Airlines case is an exposure of records with no loss reported, and Beget's data loss may be a technical failure, since Izvestia's headline does not say it was an attack. Osaka's names were only possibly leaked. What the events do not share is motive or harm, and the supplier route for the supermarkets rests on advice from Italy, not on any finding.

fragments.label: An old method
fragments.text: Breaches through contractors and staff have been the common route for at least a decade, so this may be a normal pattern made visible by one very large theft that dominated coverage in Brazil, Spain, Finland and Argentina. A day with a record crypto theft will always make hacking look like the story of the moment.

horizons.label: Since 2020
horizons.text: The pandemic moved hiring onto video calls in 2020, and much of it stayed there. Recruiters, applicants and contractors became people a firm knew only through a screen and a file. North Korean groups adapted early: from 2020 American and South Korean agencies reported fake recruiters sending engineers 'skills tests' that carried malware, and in March 2022 the Ronin bridge behind the game Axie Infinity lost about $620 million after an engineer opened a fake job offer. In December 2020 the SolarWinds case showed a supplier's software update opening thousands of networks at once. After ChatGPT appeared in November 2022, a convincing letter, voice or face became cheap to produce. By these headlines the Binance theft described by El Mundo and Yle is the largest case yet of the fake interview, and the denial from Pyongyang reported by El Litoral follows earlier denials in the same form.

horizons.label: Since 2008
horizons.text: After 2008 firms cut costs by renting their computing rather than owning it. Amazon Web Services, launched in 2006, and its rivals grew through the decade after the crash, and companies handed payroll, bookings, mailing lists and building controls to specialist vendors. In 2013 the American retailer Target lost 40 million card numbers after attackers used credentials taken from its refrigeration contractor. Bitcoin's first block was mined in January 2009, and exchanges became banks without bank rules; Mt Gox in Tokyo collapsed after losing hundreds of thousands of bitcoins in 2014. Singapore's Personal Data Protection Act of 2012 and Europe's General Data Protection Regulation of 2018 made the firm that collected data answerable for its suppliers, which is why CNA's report names Singapore Airlines rather than Amadeus. Shoshana Zuboff's account of surveillance capitalism describes the same years from another side: more data held by more intermediaries, each of them another place to enter.

horizons.label: Since 1989
horizons.text: The commercial internet of the 1990s connected offices; the next step connected machines. Airline reservations were already shared: Amadeus was founded in 1987 by Air France, Lufthansa, Iberia and SAS so that each would not build its own system, which is why one supplier's breach now reaches Singapore Airlines' passengers. From the late 1990s supermarket refrigeration, heating and lighting were fitted with controllers that maintenance firms could reach by modem and later by internet, so a technician need not visit every store. The Netscape listing of 1995 and the crash of 2000 made the network ordinary, and the Mirai botnet of 2016, built from hijacked cameras and routers, showed what ordinary devices could be made to do. David Edgerton's argument that most of technology's history is use and maintenance fits the supermarket attacks: the weak point is an old controller kept online for the repairer, as the Italian advice to check supplier contacts implies.

horizons.label: Since 1945
horizons.text: The computers of the first postwar decades were state projects, and the network that became the internet was commissioned by ARPA, the agency founded in 1958 after Sputnik, to share scarce machines among trusted universities. Trust among known parties was built into its design, and security was added later. The same postwar years built the cold chain: refrigerated lorries, supermarket freezers and frozen food spread across Western Europe from the 1950s, until a city's food depended on electrically cooled stores holding a few days' stock. Ulrich Beck's Risk Society, published in 1986, described modern societies as producing risks and then arguing over who bears them when a system built for efficiency fails. The Belgian store that threw away its stock, in Liputan6's report, is that argument at its smallest: a food loss caused by software, falling on a shop that bought its controls from someone else.

readings.line: Cheap, unclaimed threats against Poland's flights, satellite links and border now draw costly military and police responses.

watch.what: Poland's government names Russian services as behind the emailed bomb threats to flights or the arson of the Starlink station.
watch.because: The join holds that these acts share a sponsor; unrelated hoaxes and a local crime would not lead to a single attribution.

watch.what: Another emailed bomb threat diverts or grounds a flight to or from Poland or a Baltic state.
watch.because: A campaign of cheap pressure repeats because each threat costs almost nothing, while one-off hoaxes would not recur within two weeks.

ahead.precedent: The nearest case is the Polish wave of 2024, when the Marywilska shopping centre in Warsaw burned in May and other arson and sabotage plots followed. In 2025 the government attributed the fire to Russian services working through hired agents and closed the Russian consulate in Kraków. That campaign used recruited people for physical attacks, and attribution took a year. The present differs because threats to aircraft need no one on the ground, so they can be repeated daily at almost no cost.

paths.name: Warsaw names Moscow and retaliates
paths.text: Within weeks the Polish government attributes the threats or the arson to Russian services and expels diplomats or closes another consulate. Poland has done this before, the arrest in Germany gives investigators a suspect to question, and Tusk's visit to the National Security Council points to a decision being prepared.
paths.sign: Poland's prime minister or interior minister says Russian services organised the threats or the arson.

paths.name: Threats spread along the flank
paths.text: Bomb threats and jamming reach flights to the Baltic states and the Nordic countries over the winter, and NATO members discuss a joint response. The SAS threat reported by NRK and the Israeli plane in Sofia suggest this is already wider than Poland.
paths.sign: A Baltic or Nordic airport reports a diverted or grounded flight after an emailed bomb threat.

paths.name: Hoaxers with no sponsor
paths.text: Police trace the emailed threats to individuals with no foreign link, and the arson to a private motive. The detention of a second suspect and an alleged foreign instigator makes a purely local explanation for the arson less likely.
paths.sign: Prosecutors charge a lone individual with sending the bomb threats and say no foreign service was involved.

ahead.decade: Over ten years defence on NATO's eastern flank points towards policing, airport security and the protection of signals and ground stations, with more money spent answering threats that cost almost nothing to make.

readings.claim: Emailed bomb threats forced a plane to land in Warsaw, a search at Chopin airport and the diversion of two Poland-bound planes from London, while an Israeli plane landed in Sofia and an SAS flight was threatened; in Poland a second person has been detained over the arson of a Starlink station, and a Turkish man has been arrested in Germany as its alleged instigator; Onet reports Kaliningrad becoming a centre of electronic warfare and Poland's GROM special forces sent to the Russian border. Each act is cheap for whoever starts it and costly for the state that must answer: aircraft grounded, airports searched, soldiers moved. Together they form pressure on Poland's air links and border that stays below the level at which NATO's treaty would apply.

events.label: Bomb threats divert Poland-bound flights
Threats to an Israeli and an SAS flight
Starlink station arson and arrest in Germany
Kaliningrad as electronic warfare centre
GROM sent to the Russian border
Poland's National Security Council meets

fragments.label: Flights to Poland
fragments.text: Yle (Finland) reports a passenger plane making an emergency landing in Warsaw over a possible explosive on board. Onet (Poland) reports a bomb alarm at Chopin airport with aircraft checked, and ABC (Australia) reports two Poland-bound planes searched after a flight from London was diverted. El Litoral (Argentina) counts bomb threats on four flights prompting operations in three European countries.

fragments.label: Flights elsewhere
fragments.text: The Jerusalem Post reports an Israeli plane making an emergency landing in Sofia after an emailed bomb threat. NRK (Norway), citing a Danish newspaper, reports an SAS flight hit by a threat.

rungs.label: On the ground and at the border

fragments.label: The Starlink arson
fragments.text: Radio ZET (Poland) reports a further person detained over the arson of a Starlink station in Poland. DW's Turkish service reports a Turkish citizen arrested in Germany as the alleged instigator of the attack.

fragments.label: Soldiers and signals
fragments.text: Onet reports that Kaliningrad is becoming a new centre of Russian electronic warfare, and explains why GROM special forces went to the Russian border, quoting that 'this triggered preventive actions'. Onet's live page reports Tusk going to President Nawrocki for a meeting of the National Security Council.

rungs.label: Cheap to start, costly to answer

fragments.label: The arithmetic
fragments.text: An emailed threat costs its sender nothing, and an arson can be bought from a stranger; the answer costs Poland diverted aircraft, searched airports, special forces and a council meeting at the presidential palace. The targets are the links Poland relies on: air routes to western Europe, satellite internet and the border with Russia's exclave. Pressure of this kind is designed to stay below an armed attack, so that no ally is obliged to respond.

fragments.label: Recruited at a distance
fragments.text: The alleged instigator of the Starlink arson is a Turkish citizen held in Germany, not a Russian. Using hired foreign nationals keeps the sponsor out of the file, and the headlines name no sponsor. Onet's report on Kaliningrad's electronic warfare places the one named Russian capability beside acts that are, so far, without an author.

fragments.label: No author, different acts
fragments.text: No headline names Russia as behind any of the bomb threats, which are a common hoax worldwide and often the work of individuals. The Sofia and SAS threats may have nothing to do with Poland. The arson is a physical crime with named suspects, the GROM deployment and the council meeting are Poland's own decisions, and Kaliningrad's electronic warfare is a military posture, not an act. What these events do not share is an actor: one is anonymous email, one is a hired crime, one is the Polish state.

fragments.label: Who is reporting
fragments.text: Much of the Polish picture comes from Onet and Radio ZET, Polish outlets that read security news through Russia, and the collection holds several of their headlines on one day. A dense day of Polish coverage can make a cluster look like a campaign.

horizons.label: Since 2020
horizons.text: In the summer and autumn of 2021 Belarus flew migrants from the Middle East to Minsk and moved them towards the Polish, Lithuanian and Latvian borders; Poland answered with a state of emergency and, in 2022, a steel fence. After the full invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, Poland became the main land route for Western weapons. Then came acts no state claimed: the Nord Stream pipelines blown up in September 2022, Baltic cables cut by ships dragging anchors in 2023 and 2024, and the fire that destroyed Warsaw's Marywilska shopping centre in May 2024, later attributed by the Polish government to Russian services using hired agents. GPS jamming from the Kaliningrad area disrupted Baltic flights through 2024. Ukraine's drone strike on Russian bombers in June 2025 used the same arithmetic of the cheap against the costly in the other direction. The Starlink arson that Radio ZET reports, with a foreign instigator held in Germany, fits the pattern of recruited strangers, and Mary Kaldor's account of wars without fronts describes the method.

horizons.label: Since 2008
horizons.text: Russia's war with Georgia in August 2008 came with cyberattacks on Georgian government sites, a year after Estonia's banks and ministries had been knocked offline during a dispute over a Soviet war memorial. In 2014 the seizure of Crimea by soldiers without insignia gave Western capitals a name for the method: action designed to be deniable and to stay below Article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty. Russian commentators answered with their own theory, that the colour revolutions after 2003 had been Western projects, which justified the same tools in return. The explosions at Czech arms depots at Vrbětice in 2014, blamed in 2021 on the same Russian military unit later linked to the Skripal poisoning in Salisbury in 2018, showed how long attribution can take. The emailed bomb threats reported by Yle and Onet are the cheapest form yet: they need no agent on the ground, and they force a search every time.

horizons.label: Since 1989
horizons.text: When the Soviet Union dissolved in 1991, the Kaliningrad region became a Russian exclave between Poland and Lithuania. Poland joined NATO in 1999, the EU in 2004 and the Schengen area in December 2007, so that its eastern border became the Union's. The same years opened the sky to civilians: in May 2000 the United States switched off the deliberate error in GPS, and air traffic, logistics and later drones came to rely on satellite signals that can be jammed from the ground. Low-cost airlines made Warsaw, Kraków and Gdańsk part of one European market, with daily flights from London of the kind ABC reports diverted. Satellite internet, used by Ukraine's army since 2022, depends on ground stations like the one Radio ZET reports burned. Onet's report of Kaliningrad as an electronic warfare centre puts the exclave of 1991 next to the signals on which Poland's flights depend.

horizons.label: Since 1945
horizons.text: At Potsdam in 1945 the victors moved Poland west: it lost its eastern lands to the Soviet Union and gained German territory up to the Oder and Neisse, while the northern half of East Prussia, with Königsberg, became Soviet and was renamed Kaliningrad in 1946. The North Atlantic Treaty of April 1949 promised that an armed attack on one member would be treated as an attack on all, and the four Geneva Conventions of the same year set out rules for armed conflict. Both texts assume force by a state that can be seen and named. Tony Judt's Postwar describes a western Europe whose security rested on a clear dividing line; Poland was on the other side of it until 1989. The GROM deployment and the National Security Council meeting that Onet reports are Poland deciding, case by case, whether acts with no visible author cross the line the 1949 treaty drew.

readings.line: Eight years into the US-China tariff war, producers elsewhere merge to compete with Chinese goods or tax them at the border.

watch.what: Another government in Southeast Asia, Latin America or Africa raises duties or taxes on imported Chinese cars, steel or chemicals.
watch.because: The join holds that border taxes are the answer of mid-sized producers to Chinese prices, so Thailand's step should be repeated elsewhere.

watch.what: A second industrial merger or takeover between firms outside China is announced with Chinese competition named as a reason.
watch.because: If scale is the firms' answer, as SCG's chief says, other mergers should be justified in the same terms as the Tata-Iveco deal.

ahead.precedent: The closest case is the Chinese steel surplus of 2015 and 2016, when Chinese steel exports passed 100 million tonnes a year, prices collapsed and governments from Brussels to Hanoi imposed anti-dumping duties within about a year, while Tata Steel put its British plants up for sale. Duties spread faster than mergers then. The present differs because the goods are cars and chemicals rather than a raw material, and because the United States is raising barriers to its allies as well as to China.

paths.name: Border taxes spread
paths.text: Over the next six months more middle-income governments, among them Indonesia, Malaysia, Brazil, Mexico and South Africa, raise duties on Chinese cars, steel or chemicals. Thailand's tax shows that even a government that invited Chinese carmakers to build locally will tax imports, and taxes are quicker to pass than mergers are to complete.
paths.sign: A second government announces higher duties on imported Chinese electric cars or steel.

paths.name: Chinese plants move inside
paths.text: Chinese carmakers and chemical firms answer the new taxes by building or buying plants in the countries that impose them, as they have in Thailand, Hungary and Turkey. This would turn the border tax into a demand for local production rather than a barrier.
paths.sign: A Chinese carmaker announces a new plant in a country that has just raised import duties.

paths.name: China limits its own exports
paths.text: Beijing agrees export quotas or minimum prices for cars or steel, as Japan accepted voluntary limits on car exports to the United States in 1981. China has little reason to do so while its home demand is weak.
paths.sign: China's commerce ministry announces export quotas or minimum export prices for cars or steel.

ahead.decade: Over ten years the trend points to higher tariffs between middle-income countries and China, and to fewer, larger manufacturers outside China, many of them partly Chinese-owned.

readings.claim: SCG's chief executive tells Fortune that China's cheap exports are 'a fact of life' and that Southeast Asia's factories must get bigger; Thailand approves steep tax rises on imported electric cars; Tata Motors and Iveco form a group with 21 billion in revenue; the United States plans to leave the Agoa trade scheme and South Africa prepares aid as US tariffs reshape its farm exports; Kenya, Switzerland and an American farm delegation each turn towards selling into China. These are the choices left to producers caught between Chinese factories selling cheaply abroad and an American market that charges more to enter. They merge to reach Chinese scale, they tax Chinese goods at their own borders, or they try to sell to China instead.

events.label: SCG says Southeast Asian factories must grow
Thailand raises tax on imported EVs
Tata Motors and Iveco combine
US Agoa exit and South African farm exports
Kenya, Switzerland and US farmers court China
Chinese cars and imports in other markets

fragments.label: The cause named
fragments.text: Fortune (United States) quotes the chief executive of SCG, the Thai cement and chemicals group, saying China's cheap exports are 'a fact of life' and that Southeast Asia's factories need to get bigger. It is the one headline in the collection that names the cause.

fragments.label: Cars at the border
fragments.text: The Bangkok Post reports that Thailand has approved steep tax rises on imported electric cars. Dan Tri (Vietnam) reports Vietnam spending over $10 billion importing cars and components. Business Day (South Africa) reviews the Lepas L6, a new Chinese brand sold as affordable luxury.

fragments.label: A merger in Turin
fragments.text: Corriere della Sera (Italy) reports that Tata Motors and Iveco are creating a group with 21 billion in revenue, and that Iveco will keep its headquarters in Turin. Handelsblatt (Germany) reports the Ifo business climate in chemicals deteriorating.

fragments.label: South Africa and the US
fragments.text: Business Day reports the South African government preparing aid as the United States plans to leave Agoa, and the agricultural economist Wandile Sihlobo writes that US tariff shifts are already reshaping South Africa's farm exports.

fragments.label: Selling to China
fragments.text: Kenya Today reports Kenya showcasing agricultural exports at the 9th China International Import Expo. UDN (Taiwan) reports Switzerland and China updating their free trade agreement, with human rights concerns causing division. Yicai (China) reports the vice president of China's trade promotion council meeting a visiting American agricultural delegation.

fragments.label: Scale, taxes or China
fragments.text: Producers outside China and the United States face Chinese goods at low prices on one side and higher American barriers on the other. The firms answer with size: SCG calls for bigger factories and Tata and Iveco combine. The governments answer with taxes, as Thailand does on imported electric cars. Exporters shut out of the American market, such as South Africa's and Kenya's farmers, look to China as a buyer. SCG's chief names the pressure; the others act on it without naming it.

fragments.label: Even Thailand
fragments.text: Thailand invited Chinese electric carmakers to assemble there, and it is now taxing imported electric cars steeply. A government that welcomed Chinese investment still protects its market from Chinese imports, which suggests that the border tax is becoming the common response rather than a choice of hostile governments.

fragments.label: Different causes
fragments.text: Tata's deal with Iveco may be about Tata's European strategy and the truck market, and Corriere's headline does not mention China. Thailand's tax may serve its own incentive scheme, which asked carmakers to build locally in return for subsidies, rather than answer Chinese prices. The Agoa exit is American policy with no Chinese cause, Kenya attends the Import Expo every year, and Germany's chemicals slump is as likely to be energy prices as Chinese competition. What these events do not share is a single pressure: one is a US decision, one a Chinese surplus, one a European energy bill.

fragments.label: One quote carries it
fragments.text: The cause rests on one chief executive's words in an English-language American magazine. Without the SCG interview the other headlines would read as separate trade stories from separate countries.

horizons.label: Since 2020
horizons.text: The pandemic years broke supply chains and then left China with more factory capacity than its own buyers could use, as property investment fell after 2021. Electric cars became the clearest case: China overtook Japan as the world's largest car exporter in 2023, led by BYD, Chery and SAIC. Thailand, long the assembly centre for Japanese makers, offered subsidies from 2022 to Chinese firms that promised to build locally; the tax on imported electric cars that the Bangkok Post reports is the next step in that bargain. The European Union imposed duties of up to 35 per cent on Chinese electric cars in October 2024, and the American tariffs of 2025 raised the cost of entering the US market for nearly every country. Agoa, which had let African goods into the United States without duty since 2000, lapsed in September 2025, and Business Day's report of a planned exit follows from that. Each of these steps narrowed the space for producers caught between the two largest economies.

horizons.label: Since 2008
horizons.text: In November 2008 Beijing announced a stimulus of four trillion yuan, spent largely through state banks on infrastructure, steel, cement and factories. It helped carry the world economy through the crash that Adam Tooze describes in Crashed, and it left China with capacity on a scale no other economy had built. By 2015 Chinese steel exports exceeded 100 million tonnes a year, prices collapsed, and the EU, the United States, India and Vietnam imposed anti-dumping duties; Tata Steel, which had bought Corus in 2007, put its British plants up for sale in 2016. The Made in China 2025 plan of 2015 set out to repeat the build-up in cars, batteries and machinery. The American tariffs of 2018 began the trade war between the two largest economies, and every producer between them has since had to decide which market it serves. SCG's call in Fortune for bigger factories is a Thai cement and chemicals group drawing the conclusion of 2015 a decade later.

horizons.label: Since 1989
horizons.text: China joined the World Trade Organization in December 2001 after fifteen years of negotiation, and its exports grew several times over in the following decade. The same years produced the preference schemes that are now ending: the US African Growth and Opportunity Act of 2000 opened American markets to South African cars, wine and citrus without duty, and became the basis of the farm trade Wandile Sihlobo writes about in Business Day. Thailand built its car industry in the 1990s on Japanese investment and became the largest car producer in Southeast Asia. Switzerland was among the first European countries to sign a free trade agreement with China, in 2013, in force from 2014, and that is the agreement UDN reports being updated amid argument over human rights. Trade agreements in these years were a route to growth for middle-income countries selling to rich ones. That route assumed the American market stayed open and that China would import as fast as it exported, and both assumptions are now being tested in the same week.

horizons.label: Since 1945
horizons.text: The General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade of 1947 cut tariffs among rich countries round after round, while newly independent and Latin American states protected their industries behind high tariffs in the hope of building them. Japan and then South Korea combined both approaches: protected home markets and state-directed credit to build firms large enough to export, a path Meiji Japan had first taken in the 1870s. Tata, founded in 1868, grew into India's largest private industrial group under the licence system after 1947; Iveco was formed in Turin in 1975 from Fiat's truck makers and others. Karl Polanyi argued in 1944 that when markets threaten livelihoods, societies move to limit them. The border tax in Thailand and the merger in Turin are two versions of that move, one made by a state and one by firms. Whether to protect an industry or to grow it large enough to compete is the question postwar development has asked since the 1950s, and Corriere's report that Iveco keeps its headquarters in Turin shows it is still asked in national terms.
